questions.question: What are the microscopic single-celled algae that live inside coral polyps and supply the coral with sugars from photosynthesis called?
questions.expected_answer: Zooxanthellae — the microscopic single-celled algae that live inside coral polyps, photosynthesize, and pass sugars to the coral.

questions.question: By how much does a healthy fringe of mangroves reduce the height of an incoming wave before the water reaches the shore, according to the ingested corpus?
questions.expected_answer: roughly two-thirds.

questions.question: What is the name of the root-like anchoring structure that attaches giant kelp to the seafloor?
questions.expected_answer: holdfast.

questions.question: Which IUCN protected-area categories cover the strictest no-take zones where all fishing and extraction are banned?
questions.expected_answer: categories I and II.

questions.question: What is the dominant salt-tolerant grass that fills temperate salt marshes?
questions.expected_answer: cordgrass.

questions.question: Which fully submerged blue carbon ecosystem spreads by cloning itself through creeping horizontal underground stems and cannot tolerate long exposure to open air?
questions.expected_answer: Seagrass meadows are communities of flowering plants that live fully submerged, spread by creeping horizontal stems called rhizomes, and cannot tolerate long exposure to open air.

questions.question: In which ecosystem do colonies of tiny animals rely on microscopic plant-like partners for most of their energy while the animals' rocky skeleton grows only a few centimeters each year?
questions.expected_answer: Coral reefs: colonies of tiny animals called polyps, which give shelter and nutrients to the zooxanthellae inside them.

questions.question: In which kind of wetland does dead plant matter pile up for thousands of years as a carbon-rich layer because decay is slow in cold, waterlogged ground?
questions.expected_answer: Peatlands (bogs, fens, and swamps) — the freshwater wetlands in which dead plants build up as layers of peat.

questions.question: Which coastal habitat is made of giant algae that have no true roots or leaves and grows best where the water is cold and full of nutrients?
questions.expected_answer: Kelp forests — large brown algae that hold to the seafloor with a root-like grip called a holdfast.

questions.question: Which ocean-management tool lets fish rebuild inside a protected area and then drift out to raise catches in the neighboring fishing grounds?
questions.expected_answer: No-take zones inside marine protected areas, which produce a spillover effect: fish sheltered inside the reserve grow large, reproduce, and drift into neighboring fishing grounds, boosting the catch just outside the boundary.

questions.question: At what rate does a seagrass hectare accumulate carbon in its soils each year, according to the field measurements in the ingested corpus?
questions.expected_answer: a rate near 138 grams of carbon per square meter each year.

questions.question: In mangrove trees, which species filters salt out at its roots and which species pushes excess salt out through glands on its leaves?
questions.expected_answer: Red mangroves filter most of the salt out at the roots, while black mangroves push excess salt out through special glands on their leaves.

questions.question: How does a healthy salt marsh keep from drowning as sea level rises?
questions.expected_answer: Marsh stems slow the moving water so that suspended sediment settles out and the marsh builds upward as sea level rises; that accretion keeps healthy marshes roughly level with a moderate rise in the sea.

questions.question: Through which predator-prey chain could a declining sea otter population turn a kelp forest into an urchin barren?
questions.expected_answer: When otters decline the urchin population explodes and grazes the kelp down to the bare holdfasts, a stripped ground called an urchin barren.

questions.question: Where do seagrass meadows and salt marshes each store most of their blue carbon, and how does that differ?
questions.expected_answer: Seagrass stores carbon in both the plant tissue and the sediment laid down beneath the meadow over centuries; salt marshes store carbon in their soils at high rates and very little in standing plant tissue, because the marsh grass dies back every winter.

questions.question: How do mangroves and peatlands differ in where they keep their stored carbon?
questions.expected_answer: Mangroves store carbon in both the living trees and the deep organic-rich mud beneath them; peatlands keep almost all of their carbon belowground, locked inside the peat itself.

questions.question: Which grows faster, a coral reef or a kelp forest, and which of the two is more species-rich?
questions.expected_answer: Kelp forests grow quickly but hold lower species richness; coral reefs add only a few centimeters of skeleton per year and are among the most species-rich ecosystems in the ocean.

questions.question: Why does ocean acidification slow down the building of new coral skeleton?
questions.expected_answer: Carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater and forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions; those hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions, making carbonate ions less available, and corals need those carbonate ions to build the calcium-carbonate skeleton that their polyps form, so with fewer carbonate ions corals add new skeleton more slowly.

questions.question: How does converting mangrove forests into shrimp ponds damage both the regional shrimp catch and the coast's protection from waves?
questions.expected_answer: Shrimp yield tracks the remaining mangrove area, because fish and shrimp pass part of their lives as juveniles inside mangrove creeks; mangroves shield the coast from storm surges and reduce the height of an incoming wave by roughly two-thirds.

questions.question: Why might a strictly protected no-take marine reserve still lose its corals?
questions.expected_answer: A park boundary alone does not guarantee a healthy reef, because climate-driven bleaching and acidified waters can harm protected reefs just as much as unprotected ones: warming seawater triggers coral bleaching, and under ocean acidification fewer carbonate ions are available so corals add new skeleton more slowly.

questions.question: Which physical structures do mangroves and kelp forests use to shelter other marine life, and which animals does each protect?
questions.expected_answer: Mangroves shelter juvenile fish and shrimp in their tangled prop-root mats; kelp forests shelter small invertebrates in their holdfasts and give cover to fish and seals beneath the surface canopy.

questions.question: According to the corpus, what happens to the stored carbon in a coastal wetland if the wetland is drained or dredged?
questions.expected_answer: Draining or dredging a wetland exposes the soil and can release the stored carbon back into the atmosphere.

questions.question: According to the corpus, why are the cold polar seas expected to become corrosive to carbonate shells first under future acidification scenarios?
questions.expected_answer: Because cold water holds more dissolved CO2 and is naturally lower in carbonate ions.

questions.question: Which species of penguin nests among the prop roots of mangrove trees?
questions.expected_answer: Not answerable from the fixed corpus: no ingested source mentions penguins.

questions.question: What is the greatest depth at which the bioluminescent deep-sea anglerfish has ever been recorded?
questions.expected_answer: Not answerable from the fixed corpus: no ingested source mentions bioluminescence or anglerfish.
